article_title: Integrating augmented reality into inquiry-based learning approach in primary science classrooms
citation: Wen, Y., Wu, L., He, S., Ng, N. H.-E., Teo, B. C., Looi, C. K., & Cai, Y. (2023). Integrating augmented reality into inquiry-based learning approach in primary science classrooms. Education Tech Research Dev, 71, 1631–1651. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10235-y
title: QIMS: an inquiry-based learning framework for leveraging the affordances of AR
description: QIMS is an inquiry-based learning framework proposed by the authors to leverage the affordances of augmented reality in teaching and learning. The article states that "In leveraging the affordances of AR, an inquiry-based learning framework, referred to as QIMS, was proposed in this study." It was operationalised into a learning package on plant reproduction for primary 5 students and evaluated against non-QIMS conditions.
requirements: Implementation requires a learning package designed on the QIMS framework, as the study developed its lessons on the topic of plant reproduction based on QIMS
constraints: Evaluated in primary science lessons with students aged 11–12; the article notes many existing studies neglected pedagogy and instructional models when implementing AR
target_learning_goals: Science learning (plant reproduction)
21st-century skills: self-directed learning, creative thinking, critical thinking, knowledge creation efficacy
examples: A learning package on plant reproduction for primary 5 students was developed based on the QIMS framework and tested in a three-condition quasi-experiment
key_sources: Wen, Y., Wu, L., He, S., Ng, N. H.-E., Teo, B. C., Looi, C. K., & Cai, Y. (2023). Integrating augmented reality into inquiry-based learning approach in primary science classrooms. Education Tech Research Dev, 71, 1631–1651. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10235-y

description: A learning package developed on the topic of plant reproduction for primary 5 students (aged 11–12), designed based on the QIMS inquiry-based framework. The article states it was developed "on the topic of plant reproduction for primary 5 students (aged 11–12) based on the QIMS framework" and served as the instructional material in the three-condition quasi-experiment.
requirements: Lessons implemented as a series of science lessons in a primary school under the QIMS framework
constraints: Designed for the primary 5 plant reproduction topic; evaluated in one primary school
target_learning_goals: Understanding plant reproduction
Inquiry-based science practices
examples: The package was used across three conditions (AR and QIMS; QIMS; Non-AR and Non-QIMS) with 117 students

article_title: Engaging ESP University Students in Flipped Classrooms for Developing Functional Writing Skills, HOTs, and Eliminating Writer's Block
citation: Salem, A. A. M. S. (2018). Engaging ESP University Students in Flipped Classrooms for Developing Functional Writing Skills, HOTs, and Eliminating Writer's Block. English Language Teaching, 11(12). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v11n12p177
title: Questionnaire for Identifying Writer's Block (QIWB)
description: The QIWB, developed by Rose (1981), is "an attitude questionnaire of 24 items that are divided into 5 subscales": Blocking, Lateness, premature editing, strategies for complexity, and attitudes. It rests on the assumption that writer's block reflects not only emotional response to fear of evaluation but also cognitive difficulties such as lacking strategies for composing complex discourse or editing too early. Administrators wishing to identify only blockers can administer just the behavioral subscales (blocking and lateness). The article reports a total Cronbach's alpha of .74 and dimension correlation coefficients from .455 to .905 supporting reliability and validity.
requirements: Reliability upon multiple administration, as reported in Table 5, to assess writer's block levels with considerable confidence
constraints: The article presents it as assessing writer's block rather than related constructs such as writing apprehension or writing anxiety
target_learning_goals: identifying and assessing writer's block levels
examples: The study used the QIWB as a pre and post measure of writer's block for both experimental and control groups.
key_sources: Salem, A. A. M. S. (2018). Engaging ESP University Students in Flipped Classrooms for Developing Functional Writing Skills, HOTs, and Eliminating Writer's Block. English Language Teaching, 11(12). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v11n12p177

article_title: Transferring skills in quality collaboratives focused on improving patient logistics.
citation: Weggelaar-Jansen AM, van Wijngaarden J. (2018). Transferring skills in quality collaboratives focused on improving patient logistics. BMC Health Services Research. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12913-018-3051-8
title: Quality improvement collaborative (QIC) as an educational model combining learning sessions, change packages, extranet sharing and on-site support
description: The article describes the QIC as an improvement-and-education method in which, per Øvretveit et al. as quoted, "a collaborative [that] brings together groups of practitioners from different healthcare organizations to work in a structured way to improve a specific aspect of the quality of their service." Most QICs use the IHI Breakthrough methodology. The studied QICs' educational approach organized learning sessions taught by change experts and subject experts, supported by change packages (booklets describing ten distinctive phases with PowerPoint files and communication tools), a collaborative extranet, and QIC staff site visits.
requirements: Series of structured meetings to learn best practices, quality methods and change topics, and to share experiences of local changes
constraints: The studied QICs focused on patient logistics: Advanced Access aimed to reduce outpatient access time to a maximum of two days; Process Redesign aimed to reduce throughput time for admitted patients by at least 20%
target_learners: healthcare professionals in hospitals participating in quality improvement collaboratives
target_learning_goals: identifying and resolving bottlenecks in patient flow
balancing demand and supply
redesigning care processes
examples: Twenty-four of approximately 110 Dutch hospitals participated in three tranches; the studied QICs ran for five years.
key_sources: Weggelaar-Jansen AM, van Wijngaarden J. (2018). Transferring skills in quality collaboratives focused on improving patient logistics. BMC Health Services Research. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12913-018-3051-8

article_title: Teaching quantum information science to high-school and early undergraduate students
citation: Sophia E. Economou, Terry Rudolph, and Edwin Barnes. (2020). Teaching quantum information science to high-school and early undergraduate students. https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.07874
title: QI4Q marble-and-mist formalism from 'Q is for Quantum'
description: The QI4Q formalism represents qubits as marbles, with white representing state |0⟩ and black representing |1⟩, and quantum gates as boxes the marbles pass through. Superpositions are represented as "mists" — clouds of entries manipulated by nine string-rewriting rules such as cancellation of opposite-sign entries. The formalism "allows them to perform calculations and discover on their own how circuits work", and its notation and color coding match IBM Q experience to ease transfer. The authors note it is a series of string rewriting rules with a bridging rule mapping the mathematical object to physical observations.
requirements: A visual representation alongside the bracket notation, which the authors say can render the material much more accessible to students
constraints: The only non-classical gate in the formalism as described is the Hadamard; gates whose unitary matrices are not proportional to integer matrices, such as the controlled-Hadamard, are not implementable on marbles in misty states
Rules for computing probabilities of configurations and for single-marble observation (wavefunction collapse) are omitted from the introductory rule set
target_learning_goals: analyzing and designing quantum circuits
understanding superposition and interference
examples: Students work hands-on problems such as the Fig. 4 exercise with SWAP and CNOT gates, and use the rules to see interference as cancellation of two black marbles
key_sources: Sophia E. Economou, Terry Rudolph, and Edwin Barnes. (2020). Teaching quantum information science to high-school and early undergraduate students. https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.07874

citation: Andreas J. C. Woitzik. (2020). Quanteninformationsverarbeitung in der Gymnasialen Oberstufe. https://arxiv.org/abs/2011.01029
title: Unterrichtseinheit Quanteninformationsverarbeitung für die gymnasiale Oberstufe
description: The article describes a teaching unit on quantum information processing for a four-period upper-secondary informatics course, built around the qubit, one- and two-qubit gates, measurement, the BB84 protocol, entanglement, teleportation and hardware realizations. Its structure mirrors the university introduction to the field, and the topic order is variable: "Ebenso ist es gut denkbar, die Einheit auf zwei Doppelstunden zu kondensieren oder weiter auszubauen, zum Beispiel für Projekttage." Materials are provided free on request.
requirements: Students need only "Grundlagen der analytischen Geometrie in reellen Vektorräumen sowie der Boolschen Algebra und Operationen darauf, die durch Gatter dargestellt werden können."
constraints: "Es fand keine Überprüfung des Lernerfolgs der Einheit statt."
"Zeitpunkt der Einheit war nach dem schriftlichen und vor dem mündlichen Abitur."
target_learning_goals: representing qubits on the unit circle and naming the classical-bit states
applying the gates X, Z, H and CX
applying the BB84 protocol and explaining strengths and weaknesses of quantum information
describing quantum teleportation
naming physical realizations of qubits
examples: Taught in 2018 at the Faust Gymnasium Staufen with twelve students in four consecutive double periods; prior knowledge and expectations collected at the start fed into the planning of double periods two to four, matched against an overview presentation of common quantum information topics.
key_sources: Andreas J. C. Woitzik. (2020). Quanteninformationsverarbeitung in der Gymnasialen Oberstufe. https://arxiv.org/abs/2011.01029

citation: Andreas J. C. Woitzik. (2020). Quanteninformationsverarbeitung in der Gymnasialen Oberstufe. https://arxiv.org/abs/2011.01029
title: Teach quantum information processing in upper-secondary informatics to present a fundamentally different information carrier and link vector analysis with gate and truth-table notation
description: The article argues that the binary discretization of information is less self-evident than today's teaching suggests, and that quantum information lets students encounter a fundamentally different information carrier. It calls QIP "ein gutes Bindeglied zwischen der Vektoranalysis der Oberstufe und der Gatter- und Wahrheitstabellenschreibweise der Informatik," with advantages and disadvantages versus classical bits worked out in a few double periods.
requirements: The text addresses "Unterrichtspraktiker der Informatik mit soliden mathematischen Grundlagen" — teachers need solid mathematical foundations.
constraints: "Diese ist derzeit nicht Bestandteil des klassischen Informatiklehramtstudiums, wodurch lediglich eine interessierte und fortgebildete Teilmenge der Lehrerschaft für den Unterricht in Betracht kommt."
target_learning_goals: understanding advantages and disadvantages of different representations of information compared with classical bits
key_sources: Andreas J. C. Woitzik. (2020). Quanteninformationsverarbeitung in der Gymnasialen Oberstufe. https://arxiv.org/abs/2011.01029

article_title: Quantum Computing: an undergraduate approach using Qiskit
citation: Gleydson Fernandes de Jesus, Maria Helo´ısa Fraga da Silva, Teonas Gonc¸alves Dourado Netto, Lucas Queiroz Galv˜ao, Frankle Gabriel de Oliveira Souza, and Clebson Cruz. (2021). Quantum Computing: an undergraduate approach using Qiskit. https://arxiv.org/abs/2101.11388
title: Qiskit as an open-source toolkit for building and running quantum algorithms in undergraduate teaching
description: Qiskit is an open-source computational framework for writing quantum algorithms in a circuit model and executing them on real quantum devices via remote access to IBM QE hardware, or emulating them locally. The article uses it as the central classroom tool, with code boxes throughout so that readers with little scientific computing experience can reproduce the methods. It comprises five essential elements: Terra, Aer, AQUA, Ignis and IBM Q Provider, of which the article uses Terra, Aer and IBM Q Provider.
requirements: Installed via the Python package manager with the command pip install qiskit, within an Anaconda/Jupyter Notebook environment
constraints: The article's applications use only the Terra, Aer and IBM Q Provider elements
target_learners: undergraduate physics students with basic knowledge of quantum mechanics postulates and no prior scientific programming experience
target_learning_goals: applied concepts of quantum computing and quantum information theory
examples: Students in the discipline CET0448 at Universidade Federal do Oeste da Bahia built circuits for logic gates, teleportation and Grover search with it

article_title: Quantum Undergraduate Education and Scientific Training
citation: Justin K. Perron, Charles DeLeone, Shahed Sharif, Tom Carter, Joshua M. Grossman, Gina Passante, and Joshua Sack. (2021). Quantum Undergraduate Education and Scientific Training. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2109.13850
title: A taxonomy of eight programmatic approaches for adding QIST to undergraduate curricula, ordered by increasing scale of effort
description: The article organizes QIST curricular implementation into eight program forms, divided into those that likely do not need accreditation (modules, new courses, summer institute, minor) and those that likely do (certificate, concentration or track, major, master's program). It states: "Below, we list a variety of solutions for providing QIST education in PUIs. The items are roughly in order of increasing scale of eﬀ ort." Table I summarizes each approach's advantages and disadvantages, e.g. modules have "Little/no insitutional overhead" but the student experience is not formally documented.
requirements: Choice of approach must fit the goals of the program, the details of the institution, and departmental strengths
Programs requiring accreditation need approval from state or regional higher-education accreditors
constraints: As of the writing, the authors know of no standalone QIST majors within the United States and industrial panelists saw no need for one yet
target_learning_goals: quantum information science and technology knowledge and skills
examples: The NSF-funded QuSTEAM project uses a modular approach across multiple institutions
A roadmap on quantum engineering programs reviewed three existing minors, one of which may be completed without a QIST-specific course
key_sources: Justin K. Perron, Charles DeLeone, Shahed Sharif, Tom Carter, Joshua M. Grossman, Gina Passante, and Joshua Sack. (2021). Quantum Undergraduate Education and Scientific Training. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2109.13850

article_title: Quantum Undergraduate Education and Scientific Training
citation: Justin K. Perron, Charles DeLeone, Shahed Sharif, Tom Carter, Joshua M. Grossman, Gina Passante, and Joshua Sack. (2021). Quantum Undergraduate Education and Scientific Training. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2109.13850
title: An undergraduate-level QIST topic and skill list extracted from industry employer needs, spanning ideal and physical qubits, algorithms, noise, coding, statistics, and research
description: The article presents an enumerated list of four topics (ideal qubits, physical qubits, quantum algorithms, noise sources) and six skills (coding, statistics and data analysis, troubleshooting, modeling, electronics, conducting research) for undergraduate QIST curricula. It explains: "In their analysis Fox, Zwickl, and Lewandowski [ 7] compiled a list of skills and knowledge sought by industrial employers. That list covers mostly graduate-level hirees. We have extracted undergraduate-level skills and topics for PUIs from it, and we have added prerequisite elements." The grain size is curriculum-wide content selection.
requirements: Skills such as coding and statistics can be embedded in courses that are not QIST-specific
Research experiences may be "research-like" experiences within courses rather than traditional standalone experiences
constraints: Students should be introduced to real physical qubit examples "though it may be diﬃcult to go into very m uch depth at the undergraduate level"
target_learning_goals: quantum information science and technology knowledge and skills valued by industry employers
examples: The quantum engineering minor at the Colorado School of Mines may be completed without taking a QIST-specific course
key_sources: Justin K. Perron, Charles DeLeone, Shahed Sharif, Tom Carter, Joshua M. Grossman, Gina Passante, and Joshua Sack. (2021). Quantum Undergraduate Education and Scientific Training. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2109.13850

article_title: Quantum Undergraduate Education and Scientific Training
citation: Justin K. Perron, Charles DeLeone, Shahed Sharif, Tom Carter, Joshua M. Grossman, Gina Passante, and Joshua Sack. (2021). Quantum Undergraduate Education and Scientific Training. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2109.13850
title: A set of relatively inexpensive and repurposable QIST laboratory experiments for advanced lab courses, plus ALPhA immersion experiences for faculty training
description: The article catalogs quantum optics experiments (spontaneous parametric down conversion, the Grangier experiment, single-photon interference with quantum eraser, Bell inequality tests), NMR experiments, computer labs and virtual experiments (VQOL), and cloud quantum computing as QIST lab options. The conversation "focused on experiment s that are relatively inexpensive and experiments that might already be in use that could have a QIST 'twist'." It also names the Advanced Laboratory Physics Association (ALPhA), whose immersion experiences give faculty hands-on expertise with a single advanced lab experiment.
requirements: Programs lacking experimental expertise can consider commercially available quantum educational lab setups, though these are generally more expensive
constraints: The learning outcomes emphasize reinforcing that physics is an experimental science and employer-valued skills
target_learners: upper-division undergraduate physics students in advanced laboratory courses
target_learning_goals: hands-on experience with quantum optics and related equipment; understanding entanglement and correlation are not the same
examples: Specific experiment-specific outcomes listed include reinforcing conservation of momentum and energy in parametric down-conversion and the ability of individual photons to take multiple paths
key_sources: Justin K. Perron, Charles DeLeone, Shahed Sharif, Tom Carter, Joshua M. Grossman, Gina Passante, and Joshua Sack. (2021). Quantum Undergraduate Education and Scientific Training. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2109.13850

article_title: Preparing students to be leaders of the quantum information revolution
citation: Singh, C., Asfaw, A., & Levy, J. (2021). Preparing students to be leaders of the quantum information revolution. https://physicstoday.aip.org/
title: IBM Qiskit ecosystem: open-source SDK, interactive textbook, and cloud-based access to real quantum hardware
description: IBM released "an open -source software development suite called Qiskit, which is based on the Python programming language, and an open -source interactive textbook that demonstrates how to use Qiskit to implement quantum algorithms on real quantum systems". Since 2016 IBM has made its superconducting quantum computers available to the public through a free cloud-based interface, enabling a hands-on approach to QIST education. The textbook covers elementary concepts through the state of the art and can be adapted to a wide range of learners.
requirements: Access to the free cloud-based interface to run quantum programs on centrally maintained hardware
constraints: Advanced learners seeking hardware depth must separately study how to control hardware, superconducting circuit layout, encoding of quantum information, and hardware limitations
target_learners: newcomers and experts from around the world, from high school students to advanced learners
target_learning_goals: designing and running quantum algorithms; understanding benefits of quantum systems for computation, sensing, and communication
examples: Students learning quantum logic gates apply those gates to create a circuit implementing a simple quantum algorithm; a full semester-long course with 27 hours of lectures and labs
key_sources: Singh, C., Asfaw, A., & Levy, J. (2021). Preparing students to be leaders of the quantum information revolution. https://arxiv.org/abs/2111.06438
